articles.title: New Democratic Senate Spells Doom for Trump's Judicial Nominees
articles.content:
In a recent edition of this newsletter, I asked whether Justice Samuel Alito would come to regret making "the same mistake" as Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who famously declined to retire from the U.S. Supreme Court when the Democrats still had control of the Senate and Barack Obama was still president. Instead, by stubbornly remaining on the Court until her death in 2020 at the age of 87, Ginsburg effectively made it possible for her replacement to be picked by President Donald Trump and swiftly approved by a Republican-controlled Senate. That's how the conservative law professor Amy Coney Barrett came to replace the liberal legal icon Ginsburg on the Supreme Court.
After this week's midterm massacre for the Republicans, we may get the chance to find out if Alito's judicial career will end on a similarly Ginsburg-ian note.
The Republicans lost big almost everywhere in Tuesday's midterm elections, but the loss of the Senate may prove to be the most painful of all in the long run, as it will give the Democrats the power to block any judicial nominee that Trump puts forward in the next two years (once the new Senate has been officially seated).
Alito, who is 76 years old, seemingly intends to remain on the bench for as long as possible. But will it be long enough to ensure that a Republican is president and the Senate is back in the hands of the GOP when he finally does decide to retire? The combination of a Republican-held White House and Republican-held Senate may not even be electorally possible thanks to this week's results until 2032. And when you happen to be in your mid-70s like Alito is, that's a long time to wait while you cross your fingers and hope for the best against the vagaries of ill health or sudden accident.
Ditto for Justice Clarence Thomas, who is no spring chicken himself at the age of 78. I can't imagine Thomas relishing the thought of a Democratic president picking his replacement. But time and fate may give him no say in the matter. As the great existential philosopher Sturgill Simpson put it, "life ain't fair and the world is mean."
One thing seems clear enough: There is less than zero chance of the new Democratically controlled Senate approving any Supreme Court nominee that Trump puts forward in the waning years of his second term. Indeed, the Senate's Democratic majority may not approve any Trump nominee to any judicial post, preferring instead to leave the federal courts under-staffed until a new slew of liberal jurists can be safely appointed.
If a vacancy does unexpectedly arise on the Supreme Court sometime in the next two years, I would not expect it to be filled until after the 2028 election.
The Supreme Court heard arguments this week in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a case that asks whether a Catholic preschool's right to the free exercise of religion is infringed when a state denies it the ability to participate in the state's universal preschool program because the school won't accept LGBTQ families.
Judging by the oral arguments, the Catholic preschools who brought the case stand a good chance of prevailing. While the Supreme Court's three Democratic appointees seemed skeptical that any kind of rights violation had occurred, a majority of the Court's Republican appointees seemed to think otherwise, and that would be enough votes to decide the case in favor of the Catholic schools. A decision in the case is expected by late June 2027.
The post New Democratic Senate Spells Doom for Trump's Judicial Nominees appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Brickbat: Who's Watching?
articles.content:
The British government is considering a plan to expand the BBC television license fee to cover people who watch content on streaming services. The proposal, informally called the "YouTube tax," is intended to prevent people from avoiding the fee by watching content on computers, phones and tablets rather than traditional television sets. Currently, households must pay the £180 ($241) annual fee to watch live television or BBC iPlayer, even if they do not watch other BBC programming. The proposal could require another 3 million to 4 million households to pay. The BBC is facing financial pressure as the number of active television licenses has fallen by about 539,000 in one year and roughly 2 million over five years. The broadcaster collected about £3.9 billion ($5.2 billion) in license fees for 2025–26 but still recorded a £121 million ($162 million) operating deficit.

The post Brickbat: Who's Watching? appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism"
articles.content:
I thought I'd pass along this smart and readable analysis from Bill Otis (Ringside at the Reckoning); as I've mentioned before, he and his coauthor Paul Mirengoff are my go-to people for hardheaded, pragmatic, but principled conservative views. They are probably on balance more conservative than I am, but I always much enjoy their legal and political commentary. An excerpt:
In an election where overwhelmingly the preeminent issue was affordability — in other and more candid words, the increasingly obvious decline in the standard of living huge numbers of people are feeling — what has Trump been occupying himself with? Here's a partial list: Building the White House ballroom (from which, in a tone deaf rendition that defies description) he gave his election post-mortem; re-doing the East Potomac Golf Course to make it a "premium" experience; building a Triumphal Arch no one asked for or thought about when they elected him; demanding prosecutions for imaginary vandalism at the Reflecting Pool; invading Greenland; making Canada the 51st state; re-naming Lake Ontario; re-naming the Gulf of Mexico; and perhaps most prominently, making sure his name gets put on the Kennedy Center even though he had nothing to do with its creation. Then there are numerous other items: Trump passports, Trump one-dollar gold coins, and "commemorative" $100 bills, to name three.
Exactly what does this Adventure in Narcissism seem like to the voter — actually, the millions of voters — who feel like they're being stretched thin? You don't need a florid imagination to answer that one. They gave their answer last night.
It's not like Trump has had no successes. He's made three excellent Supreme Court appointments. He has tackled corrosive and unjust racial preferences like no one else had the guts to. He declines to bow to transgender bullying. Objective economic data show that, whatever "feelings" may be, the economy grew at a healthy clip just this last quarter. He used force with Iran when, for nearly 50 years before him, Presidents were content to kick the can down the road as the mullahs got closer and closer to getting the atomic bomb.
These are considerable and important achievements, not less so because Trump often acts like an oaf. But his character flaws throw a wrench into nearly everything he does. It's less that he's an oaf than that he's a child, far too often content to do what's quick and easy while leaving to adults what's messy and hard. The catch is: He's supposed to be the adult. The main thing behind the failures that got Trump his butt-kicking last night is not his classlessness, his carefree attitude [toward] the truth or his gargantuan self-absorption.
It's his immaturity….
The whole thing, as usual, is much worth reading.
The post "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism" appeared first on Reason Magazine.
